rationale: A wins by a hair because it stays cleaner on what the facts can actually support. Its strongest proof line, "whether the 10% applies to subscriptions bought inside the iOS and Android apps," goes straight at the thing a real reporter would dismantle first. B is sharper in spots, but "The prevailing belief is that a 200-million-user base plus a cheap take rate is an obvious win" invents a consensus from the pitch's own fumes. That is how a contrarian angle becomes cosplay.
gaps_in_A: "Discord adds a revenue line ahead of a reported IPO" risks making a brand-new program sound financially material before adoption or earnings data exists.
"The community server becomes the creator's paywall" is a little inflated; the angle works, but the headline gets trendier than the supplied proof allows.

"The launch lands while the IPO reporting is live" assumes current, active IPO reporting from the thinner fact "reportedly preparing for an IPO." It needs source and date verification before pitching.
The next step jumps to "journalist-fit-check"; for the strongest angle, mobile billing and app-store fee stacking should be nailed down first.
gaps_in_B: "Discord is turning 200 million users into a subscription business before an IPO" overclaims conversion. MAU is not an addressable paid-subscription base, and "turning" implies traction not in the update.
"The prevailing belief is that a 200-million-user base plus a cheap take rate is an obvious win" is invented consensus. Admitting it is inferred does not make it safe.

"moderator-to-merchant conversion: unpaid volunteer community managers" adds plausible color that was not supplied. The update says server owners can charge; it does not say they are unpaid volunteers.
The next step says "newsjack-detector," which detours into finding an external peg instead of first firming up the mobile-billing proof and named server owner.
